rationale: A wins because it is more disciplined about the facts and more precise about what would make each angle reportable. Its strongest line, "the route, not the launch," gives a real regulation reporter a story spine. B has good bones, but "renting a banking license" and "then spent it on a second shot at America" are cute copy stepping over the evidence.
gaps_in_A: "Monzo's first profitable year is paying for a second shot at America" implies the profit funded the US launch; the update only gives sequence, not causality.
"The US launch is live today" assumes launch-day timing from the supplied current time. The update says Monzo is launching in the US, but does not give a public announcement date.

"A bank with 9 million customers at home is opening in the US by invitation only" is the weakest kept angle; without invite volume, waitlist size, or a named launch executive, it risks becoming launch mechanics dressed as a story.
gaps_in_B: "renting a banking license" is not in the supplied facts. A partner-bank model is real; that phrase is a loaded shortcut that a banking-regulation reporter may hate.
"then spent it on a second shot at America" invents a funding link, then the proof section admits "do not infer it." The headline is doing exactly what the note says not to do.
"A 9-million-customer UK bank tests whether its home playbook survives America" assumes a transferable UK playbook the update never describes.
"US category contest" edges toward a market-share battle without competitor, pricing, CAC, adoption, or US target facts.
